title: Diwali: the row of lamps
hook: Rama comes home after fourteen years, and a whole city lights lamps to show him the way

segments.voice: Yesterday: Navaratri, nine nights of the Goddess, and the tenth day of victory. Your line was nine nights, then the dawn. Did you refuse one small thing for one night? Day six hundred seventy-three.

The darkest night of the month. No moon at all. And on that night, a whole city does the opposite of sleeping. Every doorstep, every windowsill, every wall gets a small clay lamp, a little cup of oil with a cotton wick. The story many families tell their children is simple: Rama is coming home after fourteen years, and the people of Ayodhya light the way so he can find it in the dark. We read Valmiki's homecoming earlier. Today, the festival that grew around it.
screen: `NO MOON TONIGHT.` → `A LAMP ON EVERY DOORSTEP.` → `SO HE CAN FIND HIS WAY.`

segments.voice: Diwali is short for Deepavali. Deepa means lamp. Avali means a row, a line. A row of lamps. That's the whole name, and it's an exact description. The main night falls on amavasya, the new moon, in the month of Kartika in many calendars, usually in October or November. So the lamps are lit on purpose on the darkest night of the month. For many families, Diwali is actually five days. It starts with Dhanteras, when people buy something new, often metal, for the home. Then Naraka Chaturdashi, with its own story, which we'll meet another day. Then the main night, when many families worship Lakshmi, the goddess of wealth and good fortune, and leave doors and windows open and lit so she can come in. People draw rangoli, patterns of colored powder or rice flour, at the threshold to welcome her. The fourth day honors Krishna lifting Govardhan hill, and in some regions the king Bali. The fifth, Bhai Dooj, is for brothers and sisters. The reasons given for the lamps vary by region: Rama's return, Lakshmi's visit, Krishna's victory. Diwali's night is shared with neighbors too: Jains mark it as the night Mahavira attained liberation, and Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, a guru's release from prison, the same season. Different stories, the same small flame. And every one of them asks the lamp to do the same job: make it possible to find the way in.
screen: `DEEPA: LAMP. AVALI: A ROW.` · `THE DARKEST NIGHT OF THE MONTH.` · `FIVE DAYS, AND LAKSHMI AT THE DOOR.` · `MANY STORIES, ONE FLAME.` · then, large: `LIGHT THE WAY HOME.`

segments.voice: If it's safe and you have one, light a candle, or switch on one small lamp, and turn off the others. Look at the light for a few breaths. Then think of someone who's far from home right now, in distance or in some other way. Picture this light set in a window for them. You don't need words. Just hold the light and the person together, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Diwali. Deepavali, a row of lamps, lit on the new-moon night for Rama's return, for Lakshmi's visit, and for more stories besides.
Your line: light the way home. Today, leave one light on for someone, a message, a porch light, a seat saved, so they know where to find you. Day six hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: At Diwali, Hindu families clean and decorate their homes, draw rangoli at the door, light rows of clay oil lamps, worship Lakshmi on the new-moon night, share sweets, visit relatives and set off fireworks; many keep all five days.

original.note: Sanskrit dīpāvalī: dīpa (lamp) + āvalī (row). Diwali is the everyday form.

trapdoor: what you thought: Diwali is the Hindu new year with fireworks.
what it means: it's the row of lamps, lit on the new-moon night, for Rama's homecoming, Lakshmi's visit and more.
what a scholar hears: dīpāvalī is a compound of dīpa and āvalī; the stories attached to the night differ by region, and in some regional calendars the new year begins the day after.

notes: Diwali's month: Kartika amavasya in amanta calendars (Ashvin in purnimanta); the script says 'Kartika in many calendars'. Confirm.
Jain (Mahavira's nirvana) and Sikh (Bandi Chhor Divas) neighbors are named briefly and without comparison; a Keeper from those doors may want to check the wording.
Day 662 told the reader that Valmiki does not describe the lamps; this script presents the lamps as the festival's telling, consistent with that.
The fourth day's association with Bali Pratipada and Govardhan Puja varies by region.
